claim: The hippocampus is critical for episodic memory.
source: The hippocampus is critical for episodic memory, and synaptic changes induced by long-term potentiation (LTP) are thought to underlie memory formation.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research in the introduction section.

claim: Synaptic changes induced by long-term potentiation (LTP) are thought to underlie memory formation.
source: The hippocampus is critical for episodic memory, and synaptic changes induced by long-term potentiation (LTP) are thought to underlie memory formation.
evidence: This claim reflects established scientific consensus about LTP's role in memory.

claim: In rodents, hippocampal LTP may be induced through electrical stimulation of the perforant path.
source: In rodents, hippocampal LTP may be induced through electrical stimulation of the perforant path.
evidence: This claim is supported by established knowledge from rodent studies.

claim: Microstimulation in the right entorhinal area during learning significantly improved subsequent memory specificity for novel portraits.
source: Microstimulation in the right entorhinal area during learning significantly improved subsequent memory specificity for novel portraits; participants were able both to recognize previously-viewed photos and reject similar lures.
evidence: This is the primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data presented in Figures 3 and 4.

claim: Participants were able both to recognize previously-viewed photos and reject similar lures after right entorhinal area microstimulation.
source: Microstimulation in the right entorhinal area during learning significantly improved subsequent memory specificity for novel portraits; participants were able both to recognize previously-viewed photos and reject similar lures.
evidence: This claim is supported by the behavioral data showing improved target acceptance and lure rejection.

claim: Microstimulation with physiologic level currents is sufficient to modulate human behavior.
source: These results suggest that microstimulation with physiologic level currents—a radical departure from commonly used deep brain stimulation protocols—is sufficient to modulate human behavior and provides an avenue for refined interrogation of the circuits involved in human memory.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental results showing behavioral changes.

claim: Microstimulation provides an avenue for refined interrogation of the circuits involved in human memory.
source: These results suggest that microstimulation with physiologic level currents—a radical departure from commonly used deep brain stimulation protocols—is sufficient to modulate human behavior and provides an avenue for refined interrogation of the circuits involved in human memory.
evidence: This is a speculative claim about future applications based on the study results.

claim: The hippocampus has been implicated in episodic and autobiographical memory formation in animal models.
source: The hippocampus has been implicated in episodic and autobiographical memory formation in animal models (Devito and Eichenbaum, 2011; Ergorul and Eichenbaum, 2004; Morris et al., 1982; Squire, 1992) and humans (Squire and Zola-Morgan, 1991; Tulving, 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: The hippocampus has been implicated in episodic and autobiographical memory formation in humans.
source: The hippocampus has been implicated in episodic and autobiographical memory formation in animal models (Devito and Eichenbaum, 2011; Ergorul and Eichenbaum, 2004; Morris et al., 1982; Squire, 1992) and humans (Squire and Zola-Morgan, 1991; Tulving, 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to human studies.

claim: LTP is accepted as a neural substrate of learning and memory.
source: This idea is motivated to an extent by a long history of research on long-term potentiation (LTP), which is accepted as a neural substrate of learning and memory (Bliss and Lomo, 1973; Kandel and Schwartz, 1982) and can be induced by electrical stimulation to hippocampal afferents, such as the perforant path or Schaffer collaterals (Bliss and Lomo, 1973; Cooke and Bliss, 2006; Larson et al., 1986; Nguyen and Kandel, 1997; Staubli and Lynch, 1987).
evidence: This claim reflects established scientific consensus supported by citations.

claim: LTP can be induced by electrical stimulation to hippocampal afferents, such as the perforant path or Schaffer collaterals.
source: This idea is motivated to an extent by a long history of research on long-term potentiation (LTP), which is accepted as a neural substrate of learning and memory (Bliss and Lomo, 1973; Kandel and Schwartz, 1982) and can be induced by electrical stimulation to hippocampal afferents, such as the perforant path or Schaffer collaterals (Bliss and Lomo, 1973; Cooke and Bliss, 2006; Larson et al., 1986; Nguyen and Kandel, 1997; Staubli and Lynch, 1987).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Deep brain stimulation (DBS) of hippocampal-related targets, such as the fornix, have shown promise for modulating human cognition.
source: Deep brain stimulation (DBS) of hippocampal-related targets, such as the fornix (Hamani et al., 2008; Miller et al., 2015) and the entorhinal region (Suthana et al., 2012), have shown promise for modulating human cognition.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior DBS studies.

claim: Deep brain stimulation (DBS) of the entorhinal region has shown promise for modulating human cognition.
source: Deep brain stimulation (DBS) of hippocampal-related targets, such as the fornix (Hamani et al., 2008; Miller et al., 2015) and the entorhinal region (Suthana et al., 2012), have shown promise for modulating human cognition.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a prior study.

claim: DBS is commonly applied through pairs of large clinical electrodes (e.g., 1.27 mm diameter), which lack target specificity.
source: However, DBS is commonly applied through pairs of large clinical electrodes (e.g., 1.27 mm diameter), which lack target specificity and, hence, may affect wide and heterogeneous neuronal assemblies in nearby brain regions.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge about DBS electrode properties.

claim: Large DBS electrodes may affect wide and heterogeneous neuronal assemblies in nearby brain regions.
source: However, DBS is commonly applied through pairs of large clinical electrodes (e.g., 1.27 mm diameter), which lack target specificity and, hence, may affect wide and heterogeneous neuronal assemblies in nearby brain regions.
evidence: This is an inference based on the physical properties of large electrodes.

claim: More spatially-focused stimulation in the medial temporal lobe (MTL) could be achieved using smaller electrodes (for example, 100 μm diameter microelectrodes).
source: More spatially-focused stimulation in the medial temporal lobe (MTL) could be achieved using smaller electrodes (for example, 100 μm diameter microelectrodes), allowing higher anatomical specificity and physiological modulation of brain circuits critical for learning and memory.
evidence: This is a speculative claim about the potential advantages of microelectrodes.

claim: Targeting afferent projections may be a more specific and efficient strategy to drive downstream neurons.
source: Moreover, targeting afferent projections may be a more specific and efficient strategy to drive downstream neurons (Riva-Posse et al., 2014), as suggested by recent optogenetic studies (Gradinaru et al., 2009; Rajasethupathy et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Microstimulation mimics effects that drive neurons naturally.
source: Microstimulation mimics effects that drive neurons naturally (Fetsch et al., 2014) and has been shown in animal studies to modulate a variety of specific brain functions, depending on the site of stimulation (Hamani et al., 2008; Histed et al., 2009; Logothetis et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Microstimulation has been shown in animal studies to modulate a variety of specific brain functions, depending on the site of stimulation.
source: Microstimulation mimics effects that drive neurons naturally (Fetsch et al., 2014) and has been shown in animal studies to modulate a variety of specific brain functions, depending on the site of stimulation (Hamani et al., 2008; Histed et al., 2009; Logothetis et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to animal studies.

claim: In nonhuman primates, stimulation using microelectrodes improved face categorization.
source: For example, in nonhuman primates, stimulation using microelectrodes improved face categorization (Afraz et al., 2006), modulated motion perception with great specificity (Fetsch et al., 2014), and increased the learning rate during a reinforcement learning task (Williams and Eskandar, 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a prior study.

claim: In nonhuman primates, microstimulation modulated motion perception with great specificity.
source: For example, in nonhuman primates, stimulation using microelectrodes improved face categorization (Afraz et al., 2006), modulated motion perception with great specificity (Fetsch et al., 2014), and increased the learning rate during a reinforcement learning task (Williams and Eskandar, 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a prior study.

claim: In nonhuman primates, microstimulation increased the learning rate during a reinforcement learning task.
source: For example, in nonhuman primates, stimulation using microelectrodes improved face categorization (Afraz et al., 2006), modulated motion perception with great specificity (Fetsch et al., 2014), and increased the learning rate during a reinforcement learning task (Williams and Eskandar, 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a prior study.

claim: In humans, microstimulation of primary visual cortex has been shown to induce phosphenes.
source: In humans, microstimulation of primary visual cortex has been shown to induce phosphenes (Schmidt et al., 1996), and microstimulation of the substantia nigra can influence reinforcement learning (Ramayya et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a prior study.

claim: Microstimulation of the substantia nigra can influence reinforcement learning in humans.
source: In humans, microstimulation of primary visual cortex has been shown to induce phosphenes (Schmidt et al., 1996), and microstimulation of the substantia nigra can influence reinforcement learning (Ramayya et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a prior study.

claim: A theta-burst protocol has been shown to be optimal for inducing LTP.
source: A theta-burst protocol has been shown to be optimal for inducing LTP (Larson et al., 1986).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a prior study.

claim: LTP induction by high-frequency microstimulation of the perforant path in vivo has been shown to cause reorganization of wide hippocampal and cortical networks in rats.
source: Importantly, LTP induction by high-frequency microstimulation of the perforant path in vivo has been shown to cause reorganization of wide hippocampal and cortical networks in rats (Canals et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a prior study.

claim: Pattern separation is the ability to retrieve the specifics of past events without generalizing to similar or partially overlapping events.
source: One crucial aspect of episodic memory is pattern separation, the ability to retrieve the specifics of past events without generalizing to similar or partially overlapping events (Yassa and Stark, 2011).
evidence: This claim is a definition supported by citation.

claim: Theta-burst microstimulation of the right entorhinal area, applied prior to stimulus onset, enhanced memory specificity for photographs.
source: We show that theta-burst microstimulation of the right entorhinal area, applied prior to stimulus onset, enhanced memory specificity for these photographs.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data.

claim: During a test phase, subjects performed better at accepting photographs from the encoding stage as previously viewed, concomitant with rejecting similar (lure) photographs after right entorhinal area microstimulation.
source: That is, during a test phase, subjects performed better at accepting photographs from the encoding stage as previously viewed, concomitant with rejecting similar (lure) photographs.
evidence: This claim describes the behavioral outcome supported by experimental data.

claim: Participants were thirteen neurosurgical patients with pharmacoresistant epilepsy, implanted with intracranial depth electrodes.
source: Participants were thirteen neurosurgical patients with pharmacoresistant epilepsy, implanted with intracranial depth electrodes, who performed a person recognition task (Figure 1, Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: This describes the study participants.

claim: Stimulation was delivered through a 100 μm diameter microwire that had been targeted to the left or right entorhinal area.
source: Stimulation was delivered through a 100 μm diameter microwire that had been targeted to the left or right entorhinal area (two subjects received stimulation on each side (in separate sessions); Figure 1—source data 1, Figure 2).
evidence: This describes the experimental method.

claim: All stimulation microwires were determined to have been located in regions known to include afferent inputs to the hippocampus, including entorhinal white matter (angular bundle), entorhinal gray matter, or subiculum.
source: In post hoc analysis, all stimulation microwires were determined to have been located in regions known to include afferent inputs to the hippocampus, including entorhinal white matter (angular bundle), entorhinal gray matter, or subiculum (Figure 2, Figure 2—figure supplements 1–2, Figure 1—source data 1) (Yassa et al., 2010; Zeineh et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by post hoc anatomical analysis and citations.

claim: The subiculum contains fibers of the perforant path.
source: Because the subiculum contains—in fact, is perforated by—fibers of the perforant path, a major output of the entorhinal cortex, it was included in our sample.
evidence: This is an anatomical fact used to justify inclusion criteria.

claim: A total of 40 experimental sessions were conducted.
source: Whenever possible, subjects performed the task more than once, using a new set of images each time, such that a total of 40 experimental sessions were conducted (Figure 1—source data 1; Materials and methods).
evidence: This describes the study design.

claim: Stimulation of the right entorhinal area significantly improved performance (Estimated Mean (EM) = 0.12, 95% CI [0.05, 0.18]).
source: Specifically, stimulation of the right entorhinal area significantly improved performance (Estimated Mean (EM) = 0.12, 95% CI [0.05, 0.18]), while stimulation of the left entorhinal area had no effect (EM = −0.017, 95% CI [−0.060, 0.025]) (Figure 3A, Figure 3—source data 1, Source code 1).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by statistical analysis and shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Stimulation of the left entorhinal area had no effect on memory performance (EM = −0.017, 95% CI [−0.060, 0.025]).
source: Specifically, stimulation of the right entorhinal area significantly improved performance (Estimated Mean (EM) = 0.12, 95% CI [0.05, 0.18]), while stimulation of the left entorhinal area had no effect (EM = −0.017, 95% CI [−0.060, 0.025]) (Figure 3A, Figure 3—source data 1, Source code 1).
evidence: This is a finding supported by statistical analysis and shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Right entorhinal stimulation caused significant improvement (mean change = 0.12 ± 0.04, t(8) = 3.53, p=0.008; effect size: Cohen's dz = 1.18, CL = 0.88).
source: We confirmed that these results were robust to the precise statistical method chosen; even a basic t-test on the difference between mean performance on stimulated and nonstimulated trials per participant revealed an effect of stimulation hemisphere (t(13) = −2.98, p=0.011), and post hoc t-tests indicated that right entorhinal stimulation caused significant improvement (mean change = 0.12 ± 0.04, t(8) = 3.53, p=0.008; effect size: Cohen's dz = 1.18, CL = 0.88), while left entorhinal stimulation did not (mean change = −0.02 ± 0.03, t(5) = −0.77, p=0.48) (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Left entorhinal stimulation did not cause significant improvement (mean change = −0.02 ± 0.03, t(5) = −0.77, p=0.48).
source: We confirmed that these results were robust to the precise statistical method chosen; even a basic t-test on the difference between mean performance on stimulated and nonstimulated trials per participant revealed an effect of stimulation hemisphere (t(13) = −2.98, p=0.011), and post hoc t-tests indicated that right entorhinal stimulation caused significant improvement (mean change = 0.12 ± 0.04, t(8) = 3.53, p=0.008; effect size: Cohen's dz = 1.18, CL = 0.88), while left entorhinal stimulation did not (mean change = −0.02 ± 0.03, t(5) = −0.77, p=0.48) (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Out of 9 subjects who received microstimulation in the right entorhinal area, eight had a higher remembered rate for stimulated trials compared to nonstimulated trials, which is more than expected by chance (p=0.020, binomial test).
source: Further, out of 9 subjects who received microstimulation in the right entorhinal area, eight had a higher remembered rate for stimulated trials compared to nonstimulated trials, which is more than expected by chance (p=0.020, binomial test).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the experimental data.

claim: Stimulation was most effective for improving memory specificity when the electrodes were positioned in the right angular bundle (EM = 0.16, 95% CI [0.09, 0.22]).
source: Specifically, stimulation was most effective for improving memory specificity when the electrodes were positioned in the right angular bundle (EM = 0.16, 95% CI [0.09, 0.22]) (Figure 4A, Figure 3—source data 1; Figure 4—source data 1, Source code 3).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by statistical analysis and shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Stimulation of the right gray matter introduced a bias towards reporting positive memory, rather than increasing memory per se.
source: Stimulation of the right gray matter, on the other hand—by increasing acceptance of both targets and lures—introduced a bias towards reporting positive memory, rather than increasing memory per se.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the behavioral results.

claim: Stimulation in the left entorhinal-adjacent gray matter decreased target acceptance rates and showed a moderate trend toward decreasing lure acceptance rates, introducing a bias toward negative memory.
source: Conversely, stimulation in the left entorhinal-adjacent gray matter decreased target acceptance rates and showed a moderate trend toward decreasing lure acceptance rates, introducing a bias toward negative memory.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the behavioral results.

claim: In entorhinal/subicular gray matter, stimulation in the left and right hemispheres may introduce opposite biases.
source: Together these results suggest that in entorhinal/subicular gray matter, stimulation in the left and right hemispheres may introduce opposite biases.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the behavioral results.

claim: All reported statistically significant effects survive correction for multiple comparisons.
source: Finally, it should be noted that, although we report uncorrected p-values throughout the results section, all reported statistically significant effects survive correction for multiple comparisons (see Materials and methods), further demonstrating the statistical robustness of our results.
evidence: This is a statement about the statistical analysis methods.

claim: The right hippocampus shows increased metabolic activity during the learning of faces.
source: This suggests a possible lateralization effect for memory of people, consistent with previous results: the right hippocampus shows increased metabolic activity during the learning of faces (Haxby et al., 1996), and single-unit activity in the right hippocampus encodes different facial expressions (Fried et al., 1997).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a prior study.

claim: Single-unit activity in the right hippocampus encodes different facial expressions.
source: This suggests a possible lateralization effect for memory of people, consistent with previous results: the right hippocampus shows increased metabolic activity during the learning of faces (Haxby et al., 1996), and single-unit activity in the right hippocampus encodes different facial expressions (Fried et al., 1997).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a prior study.

claim: Imaging studies have indicated that the encoding of pictorial material involves bilateral activation.
source: While direct recordings of neural activity have shown evidence for lateralization, imaging studies have indicated that the encoding of pictorial material involves bilateral activation (Kim, 2011), and lesion studies noted a lack of asymmetry for encoding of non-verbal material (Lee et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a prior study.

claim: Lesion studies noted a lack of asymmetry for encoding of non-verbal material.
source: While direct recordings of neural activity have shown evidence for lateralization, imaging studies have indicated that the encoding of pictorial material involves bilateral activation (Kim, 2011), and lesion studies noted a lack of asymmetry for encoding of non-verbal material (Lee et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a prior study.

claim: The left hippocampus is not uninvolved during facial encoding, as stimulation of the left entorhinal area had a behavioral effect.
source: On the other hand, our results indicate that that the left hippocampus is not uninvolved during facial encoding, as stimulation of the left entorhinal area had a behavioral effect, even if it was not to increase memory specificity.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental results.

claim: Theta-burst stimulation has been used to elicit LTP in a wide range of animal models from hippocampal slices to whole animals.
source: Previous studies in animals have noted the importance of the frequency and mode of stimulation on behavioral outcomes. Specifically, theta-burst stimulation has been used to elicit LTP in a wide range of animal models from hippocampal slices (Nguyen and Kandel, 1997; Staubli and Lynch, 1987) to whole animals (Larson et al., 1986).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: This study presents evidence supporting the efficacy of theta-burst microstimulation in protocols aimed at human memory improvement.
source: In the current study, we present evidence supporting the efficacy of theta-burst microstimulation in protocols aimed at human memory improvement.
evidence: This is a summary claim about the study's findings.

claim: High frequency stimulation delivered via macroelectrodes has been shown to inhibit nearby neuronal somata, while also providing excitation to axonal projections.
source: In addition, high frequency stimulation delivered via macroelectrodes has been shown to inhibit nearby neuronal somata, while also providing excitation to axonal projections, indicating that small changes in electrode location could lead to substantially different results (Herrington et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a prior study.

claim: Stimulating in gray matter could disrupt neuronal computations, whereas electrodes that are confined to white matter may enhance excitatory drive to downstream regions.
source: For example, stimulating in gray matter could disrupt neuronal computations, whereas electrodes that are confined to white matter may enhance excitatory drive to downstream regions (Afraz et al., 2006; Arcot Desai et al., 2014; Fetsch et al., 2014; Histed et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: A transgenic mouse model of early Alzheimer's disease shows that the more focally targeted an intervention is, the more specific of an effect can be elicited.
source: In particular, a transgenic mouse model of early Alzheimer's disease shows that the more focally targeted an intervention is, the more specific of an effect can be elicited.
evidence: This claim is based on prior research in animal models.

claim: Direct optogenetic activation of specific hippocampal memory engram cells resulted in highly specific memory retrieval in a mouse model.
source: This study demonstrated that direct optogenetic activation of specific hippocampal memory engram cells resulted in highly specific memory retrieval (Roy et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a prior study.

claim: Microelectrodes have much smaller electrode contacts and affect a more localized region compared to macroelectrodes.
source: Compared to macroelectrodes, microelectrodes have much smaller electrode contacts and affect a more localized region (Arcot Desai et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a prior study.

claim: The lower current levels typically delivered through microelectrodes have been shown to excite, rather than inhibit, nearby neurons.
source: The lower current levels typically delivered through microelectrodes have also been shown to excite, rather than inhibit, nearby neurons (Afraz et al., 2006; Arcot Desai et al., 2014; Fetsch et al., 2014), as well as those downstream of the nearby axonal projections (Histed et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: High frequency microstimulation of the perforant path that induces LTP in hippocampus has been shown to cause widespread reorganization in hippocampal networks, as well as in cortical areas, such as medial frontal cortex and nucleus accumbens.
source: Moreover, high frequency microstimulation of the perforant path that induces LTP in hippocampus has been shown to cause widespread reorganization in hippocampal networks, as well as in cortical areas, such as medial frontal cortex and nucleus accumbens (Canals et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a prior study.

claim: It has been suggested that stimulation in the entorhinal white matter, but not the adjacent gray matter, might lead to beneficial effects on memory.
source: It has been suggested that stimulation in the entorhinal white matter, but not the adjacent gray matter, might lead to beneficial effects on memory (Suthana et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a prior study.

claim: Axons of the perforant path are most densely concentrated in the angular bundle.
source: This may be due to the fact that axons of the perforant path—a common locus for induction of LTP—are most densely concentrated in the angular bundle (Yassa et al., 2010; Zeineh et al., 2017) and hence a larger number would be recruited via stimulation.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: The entorhinal region includes several additional fiber tracts—including the direct projections to CA1 via the alvear path, and hippocampal efferents.
source: Although we hypothesize that LTP induced via the perforant path is likely responsible for the positive effects of right angular bundle stimulation, it must be borne in mind that the entorhinal region includes several additional fiber tracts—including the direct projections to CA1 via the alvear path, and hippocampal efferents—any of which may be affected by microstimulation, and current imaging techniques do not allow us to separate these various tracts.
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of anatomical complexity.

claim: This study presents the first evidence that microstimulation has the potential to improve hippocampal-dependent memory in humans.
source: This study presents the first evidence that microstimulation has the potential to improve hippocampal-dependent memory in humans.
evidence: This is a summary claim about the novelty of the study.

claim: Chronic neural implants that use macrostimulation to treat conditions such as Parkinson's Disease and Epilepsy have become increasingly common.
source: Chronic neural implants that use macrostimulation to treat conditions such as Parkinson's Disease and Epilepsy have become increasingly common (Fisher and Velasco, 2014; Schuepbach et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Microstimulation requires lower levels of current to be delivered, thus allowing the implant to consume considerably less power.
source: Additionally, microstimulation requires lower levels of current to be delivered, thus allowing the implant to consume considerably less power.
evidence: This is an inference based on the physical properties of microstimulation.

claim: 150 µA cathodic-first, biphasic microstimulation was applied with a pulse width of 200 µs and an inter-pulse interval of 100 µs.
source: 150 µA cathodic-first, biphasic microstimulation was applied with a pulse width of 200 µs and an inter-pulse interval of 100 µs.
evidence: This describes the experimental method.

claim: This stimulation protocol resulted in a charge delivery of 30 nC per phase and a charge density of 9.32 µC/cm2, well below the generally accepted upper safety limit of 100–150 µC/cm2 for stimulation of neural tissue through Pt/Ir electrodes.
source: This stimulation protocol resulted in a charge delivery of 30 nC per phase and a charge density of 9.32 µC/cm2, well below the generally accepted upper safety limit of 100–150 µC/cm2 for stimulation of neural tissue through Pt/Ir electrodes (Merrill et al., 2005; Rose and Robblee, 1990).
evidence: This describes the safety parameters of the stimulation, supported by citations.

claim: Participants did not report noticing any effects of stimulation, nor did they exhibit any seizures during pre-testing or task execution.
source: Participants did not report noticing any effects of stimulation, nor did they exhibit any seizures during pre-testing or task execution.
evidence: This describes the safety and subjective experience of the stimulation.

claim: Generalized Estimating Equations (GEEs) are a class of regression marginal models for investigating the relationships between clustered response data and outcome measures in a multivariate manner and a within-subject repeated measures design.
source: All statistical models were implemented in SPSS using Generalized Estimating Equations (GEEs), which are a class of regression marginal models for investigating the relationships between clustered response data and outcome measures in a multivariate manner and a within-subject repeated measures design (Data and SPSS model definitions are in Figure 3—source data 1–2, Source code 1–3; Matlab code is in Source code 4).
evidence: This describes the statistical method used.

claim: GEEs can handle different numbers of observations per subject and do not assume equal correlations between within-subject observations.
source: GEEs are a class of generalized linear models that were developed for analyzing repeated measures data (in our case, multiple experiments for an individual subject) and, contrary to the conventional repeated measures ANOVA tests, can handle different numbers of observations per subject and do not assume equal correlations between within-subject observations (Gardiner et al., 2009; Gueorguieva and Krystal, 2004; Hubbard et al., 2010; Subramanian and O'Malley, 2010), thus making this a rigorous statistical approach for our study (see Materials and methods for details)
evidence: This describes the advantages of the statistical method, supported by citations.
